claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids.
Phase separation and interfacial voids limit thermal transport in the untreated W–Cu composite.
The proposed intervention is friction stir processing followed by controlled solution heat treatment.
A solution-treatment temperature of approximately 525 °C has been used after FSP in a composite precedent.
The treatment should be performed below the melting temperatures of the W–Cu constituents.
FSP followed by solution treatment will form a graded interphase or core–shell interfacial layer in W–Cu.
High-temperature atomic diffusion can create compositionally graded and layered interfaces following FSP and solution treatment.
Enhanced atomic diffusion at the W–Cu interface will produce a gradual compositional transition.
A gradual compositional transition will reduce thermal-expansion mismatch at the W–Cu interface.
The treatment will eliminate interfacial void formation.
Improved metallurgical bonding will create more continuous phonon and electron transport pathways.
More continuous phonon and electron pathways will increase the thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The treated composite will have statistically significantly higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
Fusion divertor joints are exposed to high temperatures, high heat fluxes, and energetic neutron irradiation.
W is used as a plasma-facing material and CuCrZr as a heat sink in the relevant fusion-component context.
The hypothesis may not apply outside optimized composite geometries and processing ranges.
The optimal heat-treatment duration, precise FSP parameters, and magnitude of conductivity improvement in W–Cu are not established.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing treated and untreated W–Cu controls under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions using thermal-conductivity and interface measurements.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant conductivity improvement beyond measurement uncertainty, or persistence of phase separation and voids, is defined as falsification.
